channel.title: Ajahn Paññāvaddho Quotes
channel.description: Dhamma quotes by Ajaan Paññāvaddho, updated every 6 hours

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "When one slips down, climbing back is hard work. It’s easy to go down but difficult to get up. That’s why it is…
item.description:
The Danger of Habitual Unwholesome Actions

"When one slips down, climbing back is hard work. It’s easy to go down but difficult to get up. That’s why it is best to avoid even small instances of bad kamma; they easily turn into habits that become a part of one’s character. When that happens, one’s character becomes altered, sometimes irreparably. There is a case on record in the suttas of a man who was a pig butcher. When he reached the age of sixty, he stopped speaking and wouldn’t take his food normally. He had to eat kneeling on the ground. He wouldn’t use his hands; he just stretched his neck out and ate from the ground. I heard there was a similar case in northern India much more recently: a man who had been a pig butcher did the same thing within the last 40 years. By killing an animal, a person incurs a debt, which can mean he takes on the characteristics of that animal. So one of the consequences of killing animals is that a person tends to assume animal-like tendencies."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: In Buddhism the arrangement between the monk and his teacher is not fixed. A monk can leave the monastery anytime he likes. Whether…
item.description:
Freedom within the Sangha Rules

In Buddhism the arrangement between the monk and his teacher is not fixed. A monk can leave the monastery anytime he likes. Whether he can come back again depends on the teacher. And he is quite free to give up the monkhood at anytime. It must be like that because we observe quite ridged and strict moral rules. A person who cannot stand it and feels he is going to do something in the robe that would be extremely bad must have the option to give up the robes at anytime. It’s far better to give up the robe and then do what he wants as a layperson.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Jealousy combines hatred's resistance to others' success with greed's desire to possess what they have. Delusion provides the misunderstanding that another's gain somehow…
item.description:
The Anatomy of Jealousy, SUCCESS, and Stinginess

"Jealousy combines hatred's resistance to others' success with greed's desire to possess what they have. Delusion provides the misunderstanding that another's gain somehow diminishes us. Stinginess is primarily greed holding tightly to possessions, but there's hatred involved too, which is expressed as fear and aversion toward possible loss. Delusion blinds us to the truth that all things are impermanent anyway. Restlessness occurs when delusion creates confusion. Greed hungers for stimulation, and hatred resists every present-moment situation as unsatisfactory. Drowsiness combines delusion's ignorance of reality with a subtle aversion to putting forth effort, while greed attaches to the comfort of simply being oblivious to what's happening. Doubt is primarily caused by delusion, but it also contains greed's attachment to multiple possibilities and hatred's resistance to committing to any of them. Sensual desire is obviously greed-dominant, but delusion provides the false promise that sensual gratification will bring lasting happiness, while hatred manifests as the emotional frustration that keeps pushing for more."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "With the Path, the question is: Must all the path factors be at 100 per cent strength for the Path Moment to arise,…
item.description:
Individual Strengths in the Path Factors

"With the Path, the question is: Must all the path factors be at 100 per cent strength for the Path Moment to arise, or does it depend on the strength of the path factors that are sufficient for a certain individual?. Personally I think the strength of the path factors is an individual thing, dependent on what a person needs. What is needed for sufficiency by a person may be very strong on one factor and weak on another. What is needed is sufficient overall strength in them all; for example, when wisdom is strong, you don't need so much samādhi, but samādhi is necessary. With the other path factors present, the samādhi will probably be Right Samādhi because it said somewhere in the suttas that each factor of the path is a condition for the one that is higher than it. They are the conditioning factors. Sammāditthi is a condition for Sammāsankappa, and Sammāsankappa is a condition for Sammāvāca, and so on... Each factor is a condition for the next one."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Ultimately, forgiveness is an expression of inner freedom. It develops the ability to move through life with equanimity, unbound by the chains of…
item.description:
Forgiveness as an Expression of Inner Freedom

"Ultimately, forgiveness is an expression of inner freedom. It develops the ability to move through life with equanimity, unbound by the chains of past wounds. It is a profound act of self-awareness where we choose peace over perpetual struggle, understanding over judgment, and compassion over resentment. Ultimately, true forgiveness is not so much something we do but rather something that naturally arises when we develop sufficient wisdom and compassion. It is the fruit of a practice that sees deeply into the nature of suffering and its causes and recognizes our fundamental kinship with all living beings. Remorse, forgiveness, and guilt arise in the mind only after we've committed an unwholesome action, which means that the mind is always playing catch-up, trying to minimize the damage."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: Suppose a situation arises in your life where you are required to do something that you would prefer not to do, even though…
item.description:
Duty and the Strengthening of Character

Suppose a situation arises in your life where you are required to do something that you would prefer not to do, even though it is your duty and your responsibility to do it. Maybe you find yourself in a position where you have to tell somebody that they're sacked from their job. You don't like doing it, but it's your duty to tell them. Whenever this happens, you must always go and do it. You must never shirk your duty by getting somebody else to do it for you. Because when you get another person to do it, you are giving way to fear, and that is very bad training for yourself. You should do it for your own sake, and look on it as an important part of your mental training. It's very important for strengthening character. And it's very important training to overcome weakness in yourself.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "We can still plan for the future as long as we are fully aware that we are doing it quite deliberately now in…
item.description:
Habitual Modes of Thinking

"We can still plan for the future as long as we are fully aware that we are doing it quite deliberately now in the present. But usually we forget. We all have habitual ways of doing things. We have habitual modes of thinking, behaving, acting, seeing and understanding. These habits so often determine our mental state. Because of that, it’s difficult to realize what the truth is; difficult to bring it into the present. Even when we are focused in the present, our habitual ways are usually hovering in the background. If our attention lapses a bit, they take over straightaway. The only thing way to overcome that is to keep on practicing the modes of training in Dhamma until the situation is seen more and more clearly. Then we begin to realize how delusory those concepts of past and future are; how they are not real things at all."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "When the citta is associated with the khandhas, it is bound up with the world of constant change. The citta changes because it…
item.description:
The Impermanent Nature of the Self and the Citta’s Role in Identity

"When the citta is associated with the khandhas, it is bound up with the world of constant change. The citta changes because it must change. Because the khandhas are part of the world, they are inherently impermanent; so the citta cannot remain fixed in that situation. The citta is the one who knows. For example, when a person gets Alzheimer’s disease, his memory fades. But he still knows. Knowing and consciousness are still present, but without memory he can’t make sense of anything. ... The citta is the one that gives the idea of self. And the idea of self is not incorrect, as long as one realizes that the self is not a permanent entity. The self is always changing. The Buddha never said that there is no self. He said that there is no entity of self which is permanent. Actually, there’s bound to be a self – that’s what we all experience. But when we examine it, we’ll see that our self-identity doesn’t remain the same for two consecutive moments. It is changing all the time.",

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Consider how we experience moments of desire. We pursue a desirable object, believing it will bring fulfillment, yet upon obtaining it, the satisfaction…
item.description:
The Instability of Desire and the Incoherence of the Kilesas

"Consider how we experience moments of desire. We pursue a desirable object, believing it will bring fulfillment, yet upon obtaining it, the satisfaction quickly fades. This occurs because desire itself is unstable: it shifts its attention, clings briefly, then it redirects its focus continuously. One desire leads to another in an endless chain, never allowing us to reach a state of lasting contentment. The defilements lack coherence in their fundamental nature. Greed pulls us toward accumulation while simultaneously fostering fear of loss. Anger promises power and resolution, but it leaves us feeling depleted and isolated. Delusion offers comfortable narratives that temporarily soothe our anxieties while at the same time disconnecting us from reality."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The practice of samādhi is extremely valuable in its ability to wake us up and sharpen the mind. Samādhi pulls the mind together…
item.description:
The Synergy Between Concentration and Wisdom

"The practice of samādhi is extremely valuable in its ability to wake us up and sharpen the mind. Samādhi pulls the mind together and concentrates it. But although it fosters a very clear mind, samādhi on its own will not turn into wisdom. Wisdom must be cultivated. When concentration is firm, it’s time to start cultivating wisdom. If you have trained yourself to keep your mind on a single object, like the breath, that training can then come into play when you are investigating with wisdom. You can use the same basic principles in the wisdom practice that you developed in the samādhi practice. You may find it very difficult to attain samādhi. Nonetheless, you should try to do so. And you should use the fruits of samādhi to develop some wisdom. Wisdom, when practiced properly, can be an aid in developing samādhi as well."
